title: 32nd BEREC International Roaming Benchmark Data and Monitoring Report (BoR (26) 28)
method: descriptive statistics from mandatory operator data collection (Art. 21(2) Roaming Regulation) plus NRA/operator questionnaires on fair use, transparency and QoS
outcomes: retail and wholesale roaming prices, roaming volumes, fair-use policy and transparency compliance
headline: EEA average wholesale data roaming price fell from EUR 0.67/GB (Q4 2024) to EUR 0.57/GB (Q3 2025), staying below the regulated caps (EUR 1.30/GB in Q3 2025 per the report's table); 91% of roaming providers inform users of regulated and alternative tariffs.
summary_plain: The EU telecoms regulators' body tracks what operators charge each other and customers for roaming. Wholesale prices for mobile data abroad kept falling and stayed well under the legal maximums, and most operators meet the transparency rules.
period_geography: EU/EEA, Q4 2020 to Q3 2025 (focus Q4 2024 to Q3 2025)
quality: Official monitoring data, broad coverage; descriptive only, no counterfactual; BEREC notes data gaps from some operators.

title: Eurobarometer survey report on the end of roaming
venue: Flash Eurobarometer / Shaping Europe's digital future library
method: telephone survey of about 26,000 respondents aged 15+ in all 28 Member States
outcomes: awareness of roam-like-at-home, perceived benefit, mobile use while travelling in the EU
headline: 69% of respondents believed the end of roaming charges would benefit them personally or someone close to them; awareness rose with travel after 15 June 2017.
summary_plain: A large EU-wide phone survey a year after roaming charges were abolished found most people knew about the change and expected to benefit from it.
period_geography: EU28, travel after 15 June 2017; published July 2018
quality: Concerns the 2017 roam-like-at-home rules that the 2022 recast extends (predecessor provision); perceptions survey, no counterfactual; only landing page read.
interested_party: European Commission (DG CNECT) assessing its own policy

authors: Arjan Premti, Mohammad Jafarinejad, Henry Balani
title: The impact of the Fourth Anti-Money Laundering Directive on the valuation of EU banks
venue: Research in International Business and Finance, vol. 57
method: event study of bank stock returns around eight 4AMLD milestones (2013-2015) plus cross-sectional regressions
headline: Across eight 4AMLD events from February 2013 to June 2015, the directive had a positive valuation effect on European banks and reduced their systematic risk, more so for larger, riskier and more profitable banks.
summary_plain: Investors reacted to the EU's 2015 anti-money-laundering directive by valuing European bank shares more highly, especially larger and riskier banks, suggesting markets saw the rules as reducing risk.
quality: Predecessor directive (4AMLD) whose customer due diligence rules the AMLR now consolidates; event study captures expectations, not realised effects; doi 10.1016/j.ribaf.2021.101397.

authors: Cécile Volten, Michel van Eeten, Rolf van Wegberg
title: Money for Nothing, Supervision for a Fee: Investigating the Effects of the 5th Anti-Money Laundering Directive on Cryptocurrency Exchanges in the Netherlands
venue: European Journal on Criminal Policy and Research
method: mixed methods: analysis of over 335,000 exchange transactions plus seven interviews with Dutch crypto exchanges and the supervisor
outcomes: compliance burden and fees on crypto exchanges, money-laundering risk exposure
headline: Dutch implementation of AMLD5 imposed high administrative burdens and substantial fees on relatively small exchanges that did not pose high money-laundering risks (analysis of 335,000+ transactions).
summary_plain: When the EU brought crypto exchanges under anti-money-laundering rules, Dutch exchanges faced heavy paperwork and supervision fees, even though the small ones studied were not very risky.
quality: Predecessor provision (AMLD5 obliged-entity status for crypto providers, carried into AMLR); single country, descriptive mixed methods, no counterfactual.

title: Results of the Survey on the designation and position of the data protection officer in the EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies
method: supervisory questionnaire survey, 69 responses covering 71 EU institutions, bodies and agencies (March 2023)
outcomes: DPO resources, independence, involvement, compliance with Regulation 2018/1725
headline: Almost half of the 69 DPOs say their resources are insufficient, 30% have no full-time-equivalent support and under 30% have their own budget, while most are consulted on 75-100% of data protection issues; 3 of 69 (4%) report being penalised for their work.
summary_plain: The EU's own data protection watchdog surveyed privacy officers in EU bodies: they are generally consulted and listened to, but many lack staff and time, which risks weakening data protection inside EU institutions.
period_geography: EU institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, 2023
quality: Self-reported supervisory survey with near-full coverage; descriptive, no before/after comparison.
interested_party: EDPS is the supervisor under the Regulation

authors: Sofie Voigt, Alinka Rother, Liadán Sage (ÖFIT, Fraunhofer FOKUS)
title: The Single Digital Gateway Regulation - Lessons from Implementation in Five EU Countries
method: structured qualitative assessment: interviews with twelve experts from Germany, Austria, Ireland, Spain and Sweden
outcomes: implementation status, organisational challenges in national SDGR rollout
headline: No EU Member State fully implemented the Single Digital Gateway Regulation by the end-2023 deadline; interviewees cite unclear interpretation, weak coordination and limited resources.
summary_plain: Researchers interviewed officials in five countries and found that none had fully delivered the EU's one-stop online portal rules on time, mainly because of coordination and resource problems.
quality: Qualitative, 12 interviews, no quantitative outcome measure; publicly funded German research centre.
interested_party: publicly funded (German federal ministry-backed Fraunhofer centre)

title: eGovernment Benchmark 2025
method: mystery-shopper measurement of 14,104 government websites across EU27, nine life events, 20 indicators (Nov 2024), with new SDGR compliance indicators
outcomes: online availability of SDGR procedures, cross-border vs national service quality, OOTS availability
headline: 93% of Single Digital Gateway procedures are available online, but cross-border users benefit less than national users and the Once-Only Technical System was not yet available.
summary_plain: A large check of EU government websites found almost all the procedures the gateway rules require are now online, but people from other EU countries still get a worse service and automatic document sharing between countries is not working yet.
quality: Large systematic measurement, descriptive; only the publisher's press release read, not the full report.
interested_party: consultancy contractor for the European Commission
